record.mistake: Wrote 'they was' instead of 'they were'.
record.rule: The pronoun 'they' takes 'were' in the past.
record.example: They was still very tired after the long trip but happy about the whole weekend.

record.mistake: Wrote 'tell to the driver' with an extra preposition.
record.rule: The verb 'tell' takes its object directly, without 'to'.
record.example: Please tell to the driver that we will wait outside the main gate at noon.

record.mistake: Used a stative verb in the continuous form.
record.rule: Stative verbs like 'know' are not used in the continuous.
record.example: My sister is knowing the answer but she does not want to tell it me.

record.mistake: Used the present simple with 'since' for a continuing state.
record.rule: A state continuing from the past takes the present perfect.
record.example: I am here since one hour and nobody from the office has opened the door.

record.mistake: Used the future tense inside an indirect question and dropped an article.
record.rule: An indirect question keeps normal tense rules, and countable nouns need articles.
record.example: The customer asked when the update will arrive and nobody could give him clear answer.

record.mistake: Wrote 'discussed about' with a redundant preposition.
record.rule: The verb 'discuss' takes a direct object without 'about'.
record.example: We discussed about the schedule for a long time without reaching any decision at all.

record.mistake: Wrote 'is agree' with an unnecessary auxiliary.
record.rule: The verb 'agree' is not combined with 'be'.
record.example: The team is agree that the plan needs more work before we can show it.

record.mistake: Used a plural noun after 'every'.
record.rule: The determiner 'every' takes a singular noun.
record.example: Every members of the group must bring their own notes to the next session please.

record.mistake: Used the infinitive after 'look forward to'.
record.rule: The phrase 'look forward to' takes a gerund.
record.example: I am looking forward to hear from you about the plan.

record.mistake: Used 'said me' instead of 'told me'.
record.rule: Use 'tell' with a person as the object; 'say' takes the words said.
record.example: She said me that she would call back after lunch.

record.mistake: Used 'will' inside an 'if' clause and 'like' for 'as'.
record.rule: A first conditional keeps the present tense after 'if', and 'as planned' is the fixed phrase.
record.example: If it will rain tomorrow, we will continue like planned.

record.mistake: Used 'furnitures' as a plural countable noun.
record.rule: The noun 'furniture' is uncountable and has no plural form.
record.example: We carried too many furnitures into the small room.

record.mistake: Dropped the third-person '-s' twice in one sentence.
record.rule: A present-tense verb takes '-s' with a third-person singular subject.
record.example: He don't like cold coffee, so he always drink tea.

record.mistake: Mixed singular and plural verbs with indefinite pronouns.
record.rule: The pronoun 'everyone' takes a singular verb; 'people' takes a plural verb.
record.example: Everyone are welcome, even people who has never joined before.

record.mistake: Used the present simple with 'since' for a continuing activity.
record.rule: An activity continuing from the past takes the present perfect.
record.example: They work together since many years in the same office.

record.mistake: Used 'remember' when 'remind' was meant, and dropped an '-s'.
record.rule: Someone reminds you of something, and singular subjects take '-s' verbs.
record.example: Please remember me about the meeting before the phone start ringing.

record.mistake: Used 'hates' with the plural subject 'they both'.
record.rule: A plural subject takes a plural verb.
record.example: I have 2 cats and they both hates the vacuum robot.

record.mistake: Placed 'more' after the noun.
record.rule: The word 'more' comes before the noun it modifies.
record.example: We need 12 chairs more for the workshop room.

record.mistake: Used 'are' with a singular chapter number.
record.rule: A single chapter takes a singular verb.
record.example: Chapter 7 are the most difficult part of the book.

record.mistake: Wrote 'without to call' instead of 'without calling'.
record.rule: The preposition 'without' takes a gerund.
record.example: He arrived at 9 in the morning without to call first.

record.mistake: Used a singular noun after a plural number.
record.rule: Numbers greater than one take a plural noun.
record.example: The test has 20 question in total.

record.mistake: Used 'person' after a plural number.
record.rule: The plural of 'person' in ordinary prose is 'people'.
record.example: Only 5 person came to the rehearsal yesterday.

record.mistake: Used a cardinal number for a floor.
record.rule: Floors take ordinal numbers: 'the third floor'.
record.example: She is living on the 3 floor of our building.

record.mistake: Used a singular noun after 'forty-five'.
record.rule: Numbers greater than one take a plural noun.
record.example: We waited 45 minute for the last bus.

record.mistake: Used the adjective 'good' where the adverb was needed.
record.rule: An adverb modifies a verb: 'reads well'.
record.example: My son is 6 years and already reads good.

record.mistake: Used 'have' with a singular page number.
record.rule: A single page takes a singular verb.
record.example: Page 88 have a typo in the second line.

record.mistake: Wrote 'can to park' with an extra 'to'.
record.rule: Modal verbs take the base form without 'to'.
record.example: You can to park here after lunch if the gate is open.

record.mistake: Used the present simple with 'since' for a continuing state.
record.rule: A state continuing from the past takes the present perfect.
record.example: The picture hangs above the sofa since we moved in.

record.mistake: Wrote 'the informations you asked are here attached' in a reply.
record.rule: The noun 'information' is uncountable and has no plural form.
record.example: The information you asked for is attached.

record.mistake: Used the adjective 'quick' where the adverb was needed.
record.rule: An adverb modifies a verb: 'come quickly'.
record.example: Come here quick, the cake is almost ready.

record.mistake: Used 'walking' where 'on foot' or 'a walk' fits.
record.rule: Distances are described as 'a ten-minute walk'.
record.example: From here to the station is only ten minutes walking.

record.mistake: Said 'the box what is above the fridge' in a voice note.
record.rule: Use 'that' or 'which' in relative clauses, never bare 'what'.
record.example: The box that is above the fridge is empty.

record.mistake: Used the present perfect with 'yesterday'.
record.rule: A finished time expression takes the past simple.
record.example: I was tired; nevertheless I have finished the whole draft before midnight yesterday.

record.mistake: Wrote 'catched' as the past of 'catch'.
record.rule: The past of 'catch' is 'caught'.
record.example: The train was late; we catched the next one instead.

record.mistake: Joined two full sentences with only a comma.
record.rule: Use a semicolon between close clauses; a comma alone is too weak.
record.example: It was late, we went home anyway.

record.mistake: Dropped the third-person '-s' on 'prefer'.
record.rule: A present-tense verb takes '-s' with a singular subject.
record.example: She likes tea; her brother prefer coffee.

record.mistake: Wrote 'the demo failed; we has rescheduled it' in the update.
record.rule: The pronoun 'we' takes 'have', never 'has'.
record.example: The demo failed; we have rescheduled it.

record.mistake: Used 'don't' with a third-person singular subject.
record.rule: Third-person singular negatives use 'doesn't'.
record.example: Bring your laptop; the projector don't accept phones.

record.mistake: Used the noun 'worry' where the adjective was needed.
record.rule: After 'be', use the adjective 'worried'.
record.example: Sales grew by five percent but the team was still worry.

record.mistake: Wrote 'costed' as the past of 'cost'.
record.rule: The verb 'cost' keeps the same form in the past.
record.example: The ticket costed forty dollars at the door.

record.mistake: Used 'has' with the plural subject 'users'.
record.rule: A plural subject takes 'have'.
record.example: Nearly half of the users has never opened the settings.

record.mistake: Used 'with changing' instead of 'by changing'.
record.rule: Use 'by' plus a gerund for the means of doing something.
record.example: We saved almost two hundred euros with changing the supplier.

record.mistake: Dropped the third-person '-s' on 'happen'.
record.rule: A present-tense verb takes '-s' with a singular subject.
record.example: A third of the group were absent, which happen every Monday.

record.mistake: Wrote 'thanks God' instead of 'thank God'.
record.rule: The fixed expression is 'thank God'.
record.example: Thank God the files were backed up.

record.mistake: Mixed 'how it looks' and 'what it looks like'.
record.rule: Say 'what it looks like' or 'how it looks', not a blend of both.
record.example: Show me what it looks like.

record.mistake: Wrote 'more angry' instead of 'angrier'.
record.rule: Short adjectives form the comparative with '-er'.
record.example: He was angrier than before.

record.mistake: Omitted the article before a singular countable noun.
record.rule: A singular countable noun needs an article or another determiner.
record.example: I sent you a report yesterday.

record.mistake: Used 'the' before a general plural noun.
record.rule: General plural nouns take no article in English.
record.example: Engineers enjoy solving hard problems.

record.mistake: Used 'informations' as a plural countable noun.
record.rule: The noun 'information' is uncountable and has no plural form.
record.example: This information is very useful.

record.mistake: Used 'advices' as a plural form.
record.rule: The noun 'advice' is uncountable; one item is 'a piece of advice'.
record.example: She gave me useful advice about the move.

record.mistake: Wrote 'depends from' instead of 'depends on'.
record.rule: The verb 'depend' takes the preposition 'on'.
record.example: The outcome depends on the weather.

record.mistake: Wrote 'married with' instead of 'married to'.
record.rule: A person is married to someone, not married with someone.
record.example: He is married to a teacher.

record.mistake: Used 'in the weekend' instead of 'at the weekend'.
record.rule: British English says 'at the weekend'; American English says 'on the weekend'.
record.example: We often hike at the weekend.

record.mistake: Wrote 'discuss about' with a redundant preposition.
record.rule: The verb 'discuss' takes a direct object without 'about'.
record.example: Let us discuss the schedule tomorrow.

record.mistake: Wrote 'explain me' instead of 'explain to me'.
record.rule: The verb 'explain' needs 'to' before an indirect object.
record.example: Please explain the change to me.

record.mistake: Used a past form after 'did' in a question.
record.rule: Questions with 'did' take the base form of the verb.
record.example: Did you finish the draft?

record.mistake: Dropped the third-person '-s' on a present-tense verb.
record.rule: A present-tense verb takes '-s' with a third-person singular subject.
record.example: She writes very clear summaries.

record.mistake: Used the present perfect with a finished-time adverbial.
record.rule: A finished time expression takes the past simple, not the present perfect.
record.example: I visited my aunt last spring.

record.mistake: Used 'will' inside an 'if' clause.
record.rule: A first conditional keeps the present tense in the 'if' clause.
record.example: If it rains, we will stay inside.

record.mistake: Wrote 'I am agree' instead of 'I agree'.
record.rule: The verb 'agree' is not used with 'be'.
record.example: I agree with your plan.

record.mistake: Used the infinitive after 'look forward to'.
record.rule: The phrase 'look forward to' takes a gerund.
record.example: I look forward to seeing you soon.

record.mistake: Used a gerund after 'decide'.
record.rule: The verb 'decide' takes an infinitive.
record.example: They decided to postpone the trip.

record.mistake: Wrote 'stop to smoke' when the activity was meant to end.
record.rule: Use a gerund after 'stop' when the activity itself ends.
record.example: He stopped smoking last year.

record.mistake: Wrote 'do a photo' instead of 'take a photo'.
record.rule: English speakers take photos rather than do them.
record.example: She took a photo of the sunset.

record.mistake: Wrote 'make a party' instead of 'have a party'.
record.rule: English speakers have or throw a party, not make one.
record.example: We had a small party for her birthday.

record.mistake: Wrote 'open the light' instead of 'turn on the light'.
record.rule: Lights are turned on and off, not opened and closed.
record.example: Please turn on the light.

record.mistake: Placed the adverb between the verb and its object.
record.rule: An adverb of manner does not separate a verb from its direct object.
record.example: She speaks English fluently.

record.mistake: Used question word order in an embedded question.
record.rule: An embedded question keeps statement word order.
record.example: I wonder where the meeting is.

record.mistake: Placed 'always' after the main verb.
record.rule: Frequency adverbs come before the main verb but after 'be'.
record.example: He always arrives early.

record.mistake: Used 'much' with a countable plural noun.
record.rule: Use 'many' with countable nouns and 'much' with uncountable nouns.
record.example: How many chairs do we need?

record.mistake: Used 'less' with a countable plural noun.
record.rule: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns and 'less' with uncountable nouns.
record.example: We received fewer complaints this month.

record.mistake: Treated 'furniture' as a countable noun.
record.rule: The noun 'furniture' is uncountable; count pieces of furniture instead.
record.example: The room has too much furniture.

record.mistake: Used 'actual' to mean 'current'.
record.rule: In English 'actual' means real, not current; use 'current' for the present state.
record.example: The current version works well.

record.mistake: Used 'eventually' to mean 'possibly'.
record.rule: In English 'eventually' means in the end, not possibly.
record.example: The team eventually agreed on a design.

record.mistake: Used 'sympathetic' to mean 'likeable'.
record.rule: In English 'sympathetic' means showing compassion; a likeable person is 'friendly'.
record.example: Our new colleague is very friendly.

record.mistake: Used 'control' to mean 'check'.
record.rule: Use 'check' for verifying something; 'control' means to direct or regulate.
record.example: Please check the totals before sending.

record.mistake: Used a plural verb with 'everyone'.
record.rule: Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone' take a singular verb.
record.example: Everyone is welcome to join.

record.mistake: Used 'peoples' as the plural of 'people'.
record.rule: The word 'people' is already plural; 'peoples' refers to ethnic groups.
record.example: Many people attended the talk.

record.mistake: Wrote 'more easy' instead of 'easier'.
record.rule: Short adjectives form the comparative with '-er'.
record.example: This route is easier in daylight.

record.mistake: Doubled the comparative with 'more better'.
record.rule: A comparative adjective is not combined with 'more'.
record.example: The second draft is better.

record.mistake: Used the present simple for a state that started in the past and continues.
record.rule: Use the present perfect for a state that began in the past and continues now.
record.example: I have lived in this city for ages.

record.mistake: Used 'since' with a duration.
record.rule: Use 'for' with durations and 'since' with starting points.
record.example: They have worked together for years.

record.mistake: Used 'must' for a polite suggestion.
record.rule: Use 'should' for advice; 'must' expresses strong obligation.
record.example: You should try the earlier train.

record.mistake: Wrote 'can to' before a verb.
record.rule: Modal verbs are followed by the base form without 'to'.
record.example: She can swim very well.

record.mistake: Said 'he don't' instead of 'he doesn't'.
record.rule: Third-person singular negatives use 'doesn't'.
record.example: He doesn't like cold coffee.

record.mistake: Used 'borrow' when 'lend' was meant.
record.rule: You borrow something from someone and lend something to someone.
record.example: Can you lend me your umbrella?

record.mistake: Used 'remember' when 'remind' was meant.
record.rule: Someone reminds you of something; you remember it yourself.
record.example: Please remind me about the meeting.

record.mistake: Used 'say' with a person as the object.
record.rule: Use 'tell' with a person as the object; 'say' takes the words said.
record.example: She told me the news.

record.mistake: Wrote 'I have cold' without an article.
record.rule: The expression is 'have a cold', with an article.
record.example: I have a cold and will rest.

record.mistake: Used 'too' when 'very' was meant.
record.rule: The word 'too' signals excess; 'very' is neutral emphasis.
record.example: The lecture was very interesting.

record.mistake: Confused 'lose' and 'loose'.
record.rule: The verb meaning to misplace is 'lose'; 'loose' is an adjective.
record.example: Do not lose the spare key.

record.mistake: Wrote 'in the end of' instead of 'at the end of'.
record.rule: Use 'at the end of' for position; 'in the end' means finally.
record.example: The summary is at the end of the report.

record.mistake: Used 'until' when 'by' was meant.
record.rule: Use 'by' for deadlines and 'until' for continuing states.
record.example: Please reply by Friday.

record.mistake: Wrote 'near to' with an unnecessary preposition.
record.rule: The word 'near' is used without 'to' before a place.
record.example: The bakery is near the station.

record.mistake: Wrote 'kindly revert' to mean 'reply'.
record.rule: In standard English 'revert' means going back to a previous state, not replying.
record.example: Please reply when you have news.

record.mistake: Used 'learn' when 'teach' was meant.
record.rule: You teach something to others and learn it yourself.
record.example: She teaches beginners every winter.
